assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed how trade is modeled and measured. It moved the field from representative-firm models to models in which trade reallocates activity across firms. The framework is a standard workhorse in theory, empirics and policy analysis. It also generated new welfare and distributional channels.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central selection model, and Helpman with Melitz and Yeaple (2004) gave the export-versus-FDI sorting result. Helpman's wider contributions to the theory of trade also support the credit. Redding is an important later contributor to quantitative and spatial extensions, but I judge the core credit to rest with the first two.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of replication, extension and structural and reduced-form testing. The core predictions have been checked repeatedly in firm-level data across many countries. The idea is well established and not recent.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to pair this with the Eaton-Kortum or quantitative trade tradition, or with Grossman-Helpman (B047).
Redding's marginal claim relative to the other two.
The Melitz model's welfare implications depend on distributional assumptions, and the literature has debated them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work links optimal tax theory to empirically estimable sufficient statistics, in particular the elasticity of taxable income and bunching methods. It changed how tax policy is evaluated and has had large policy influence. It combines theory and credible empirics.
assessment.attribution: Saez is the clearest anchor, for the optimal-tax and elasticity-of-taxable-income work. Chetty is central to the sufficient-statistics approach. Slemrod and Stantcheva contributed importantly, but the credit is spread across a large group and the three-laureate cap forces choices. Chetty's other work (B039) overlaps with this candidate.
assessment.maturity: The elasticity and bunching literatures are well developed, and the policy uptake is clear. Some newer contributions are still being evaluated.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse, and Mirrlees and Diamond's earlier recognition affects how the committee frames the novelty.
Elasticity estimates vary with context, and some identification strategies have been challenged.
Overlap in Chetty's and Saez's names with B039 and B044 may complicate how the committee packages the work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the New Keynesian framework and policy rules are the core of modern monetary policy analysis. They underpin inflation targeting and central bank practice. The impact on both theory and policy is very large.
assessment.attribution: Calvo supplied the time-dependent pricing device, Taylor the staggered-contract and policy-rule work, and Woodford the integrated microfounded framework. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets were also central, particularly for estimation and DSGE implementation. The list is very crowded, so any three-person selection will omit significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: Decades old and deeply embedded. The post-2008 and post-2020 inflation episodes have prompted reassessment, but this strengthens the case for recognizing the framework's foundations.
uncertainties: Credit is very diffuse, and any three-person selection is contestable.
The framework's performance in recent inflation episodes is debated.
Taylor-rule and Calvo-pricing attribution could be argued differently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work turned adverse-selection theory into measurable, welfare-relevant objects in real insurance markets. It combines credible, often quasi-experimental or randomized, designs with structural welfare analysis. It informs health insurance policy and market design.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the most consistent joint contributors. They did the empirical measurement of selection and moral hazard and the welfare analysis of selection markets. Salanie's contribution to testing for asymmetric information in insurance is real, but the credit is more about methods. The theoretical foundations belong to earlier laureates (Akerlof, Rothschild-Stiglitz, Spence).
assessment.maturity: The measurement program is well developed but still recent relative to the older candidates, and the fullest policy and welfare conclusions are still being refined.
uncertainties: Distinguishing the empirical contribution from earlier Nobel-recognized theory.
Whether the committee will see this as sufficiently mature relative to older candidates.
Generalization of findings across institutional settings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work changed how economists understand technological change and trade exposure in labor markets. It established persistent local labor market adjustment costs after trade shocks and developed a tasks-based view of labor demand. It has had major academic and policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the tasks and the trade-shock strands. Hanson, together with Autor and Dorn, is central to the China-shock evidence. Katz contributed greatly to the earlier skill-premium and technology work, and Dorn to the trade-shock papers, so a two-person selection omits some important credit. The tasks framework also draws on contributors outside this list.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock work is about a decade old and has been extensively replicated, extended and debated. Its core adjustment-cost findings have held up, though some interpretive questions remain.
uncertainties: Debate over magnitudes and interpretation of the China shock, including specification and instrument choices.
Overlap with tasks-based work by authors not on the list.
Credit among four named contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework provided a quantitative, tractable way to link micro-level distortions to aggregate TFP differences across countries. It reorganized much of the development accounting and growth literature. It is also influential in policy-oriented work on firm dynamics and reform.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the pivotal paper and is clearly the main credit. Restuccia and Rogerson's earlier and parallel contributions are important, and Restuccia is the third name on this list. The measurement relies heavily on assumptions, so the credit is partly conceptual and partly methodological.
assessment.maturity: Roughly fifteen years of use, with extensive extensions and critiques. The influence is clear, but the interpretation of measured misallocation continues to be debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error and model-dependence can inflate or deflate estimated misallocation.
Parallel credit to Restuccia and Rogerson.
Whether it is mature enough relative to other candidates and how it relates to the 2025 growth prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence field experiments gave transparent, credible causal evidence of labor-market discrimination. The resume-callback design became a template across economics and social science. The methodological and substantive influence is large and it is policy-relevant.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004) is the best-known study and anchors the credit. Charles's work with Guryan on prejudice and wages is a separate, important contribution. The audit-study tradition predates and extends beyond these authors, which complicates attribution. Mullainathan's broader behavioral work could also draw credit.
assessment.maturity: The design has been replicated many times in many countries and settings, and meta-analyses largely support the existence of discrimination. Debate continues about mechanisms (taste-based versus statistical) and about interpretation of callback gaps.
uncertainties: Attribution relative to earlier audit-study pioneers outside the list.
Callback differences do not map cleanly onto labor-market outcomes, and mechanisms are hard to identify.
Whether the committee prefers to recognize the broader discrimination literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design created a unified framework for how a sender should optimally structure information. It connects to mechanism design and communication, and applies to markets, regulation, disclosure and platform design. It is a substantial theoretical contribution with growing applications.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) is the foundational paper. Bergemann and Morris developed the broader information-design and robust-predictions program. Morris also has a distinct prior record in global games and robust mechanism design. A three-person cap forces an exclusion between Bergemann and Morris, and Gentzkow's other empirical work (media) is not the basis for this candidate.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen years old and rapidly developing. The theory is established, but empirical and practical validation is thinner than for the older candidates above.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees it as mature enough, given that empirical tests and applications are still limited.
Choice among four contributors, particularly Bergemann versus Kamenica or Gentzkow.
The main insights partly build on earlier cheap-talk and signaling theory.
